source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Stop sampling when a Beta model says the current majority answer will almost surely stay the majority. Same accuracy as fixed 40-sample self-consistency with far fewer samples.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models (GPT-3.5-turbo, Vicuna-13B, Code-davinci-002). Max 40 samples, temp 0.7. Math: 40 -> 13.8 samples (3.3x), acc 73.2 -> 73.1. Commonsense: 40 -> 15.8 (2.9x), 66.0 -> 65.8. Symbolic: 40 -> 13.1 (3.8x), 72.8 -> 72.8. Code: 312.5 -> 173.6 (2.4x), 35.2 -> 35.6.
limits: Savings depend on model strength: GPT-3.5 4.4x, Code-davinci 3.4x, Vicuna-13B only 1.9x. Authors say it is expected to fail where self-consistency fails. Sequential sampling raises latency.
agent_relevance: Strong sample-saving rule for our S4/S7 voting step. Saving is largest when the model is good and answers agree early; weak models save little.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: At equal average sample cost the Beta stopping rule beats fixed-budget self-consistency, because it spends more on contested questions and less on easy ones. The choice of rule matters: Beta and Dirichlet are best, a plain Majority threshold is worse, Random is worst.
numbers: GSM8K: at an average cost of 10 samples, about 3% higher accuracy than self-consistency at 10. Boolean Expressions: 7.9x fewer samples, no accuracy loss. SVAMP: comparable accuracy with under 5 samples on average. Dirichlet and CRP rules match Beta but are about 4 orders of magnitude slower (still negligible against an LLM call).
limits: Biggest gains where the answer set is small (yes/no, boolean). Threshold 0.95 was chosen high; lower thresholds stop too early.
agent_relevance: Supports G12 (spend by difficulty). A cheap Beta rule in code is enough, no model judge needed, which fits G5.

source: Li, Yuan, Feng et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR 2024
finding: Sample in small windows; stop when a whole window gives one identical answer. Cuts samples a lot with almost no accuracy change, and 99% or more of final votes equal the full self-consistency vote.
numbers: Window 5 (8 for MATH), max 40 (64 for MATH), mean of 10 runs. Abstract: sample cuts MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. Share of identical final votes, ESC vs SC: 99.13 to 99.96% on GSM8K, StrategyQA and Letters across GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2-7b.
limits: Savings rise with model accuracy. Llama-2-7b on MATH: 64 -> 62.48 samples (only -1.5); GPT-4 on MATH: 64 -> 42.4. Weak model plus hard task gives almost no saving. Window size is hand-set.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: window-agreement stopping saves least exactly where the model is weakest. Pair with a difficulty gate so low-foothold problems get a different policy (G12).

source: Li, Yuan, Feng et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR 2024
finding: ESC at the same average cost beats plain self-consistency at that smaller sample size, and a control scheme can predict cost and accuracy change before running.
numbers: MATH, GPT-3.5, window 8: SC with 16 samples 47.34 vs ESC 47.33 using 14.84 samples; at max 64, ESC 49.96 with 52.37 samples (SC 49.96). Control-scheme prediction vs actual: Pearson correlation above 0.8 for both sample count and performance change (GSM8K, varying max size). Also works on MBPP code and with Progressive-Hint Prompting.
limits: Prediction check used GSM8K only. Fixed windows assume answers arrive like independent draws.
agent_relevance: The cost/accuracy trade can be forecast offline from a small calibration run, which fits a per-class budget table.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Origin of the vote-over-samples baseline that every stopping rule above tries to cheapen. Gains over greedy CoT grow with samples and then flatten.
numbers: Not opened. Second-hand from the ESC paper: SC beats greedy CoT substantially on all six benchmarks, and sample size 40 (64 for MATH) is the standard setting.
limits: Not read directly; pointer only.
agent_relevance: Always compare a stopping rule with SC at equal mean samples, not at the max.

source: Taubenfeld, Sheffer et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weight each sampled answer's vote by the model's own confidence in that sample (softmax-normalised within the question). Same accuracy with fewer samples than plain majority voting.
numbers: 9 models, 4 datasets (MMLU-Pro, MATH, GSM8K, BBH). Cost reduction vs SC, macro average, budget 10: P(True) 46% (SC needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10), response probability 31%, verbal 0-100 30%, verbal binary 10%. Budget 5: P(True) 41%. Accuracy gain at budget 10: 0.2 to 1.1 points. Normalisation matters: P(True) 32% saving without it, 46% with it. Some configs exceed 67% reduction.
limits: Needs a tuned softmax temperature per confidence method. Accuracy gain is small; the gain is mostly in samples saved. Authors note that sequential stopping methods raise latency, while CISC keeps samples parallel.
agent_relevance: Self-reported confidence can weight votes, but only as a hint, never as proof (G4, G5). Do the weighting in code and ask the model only for a score.

source: Taubenfeld, Sheffer et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Within-question discrimination (can confidence tell right from wrong answers to the SAME question) predicts usefulness for voting; usual calibration scores do not. The best-calibrated confidence method was the least useful.
numbers: Within-question discrimination (pairwise): P(True) 62.3%, response probability 59.0%, verbal 0-100 56.1%, verbal binary 52.2% (chance 50%). Calibration after temperature scaling, ECE-t: verbal binary 0.005 (best) vs P(True) 0.030; yet CISC cost reduction was 10% for verbal binary vs 46% for P(True).
limits: Verbal methods barely beat chance (52 to 56%). Based on four methods only.
agent_relevance: Do not pick a confidence signal by calibration. Test within-question ranking on our own tasks before using it as a stop or vote signal.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Stop individual reasoning traces when a sliding-window confidence (from token probabilities) falls below a threshold learned from a warmup set; vote only over confident traces. Large token savings at about equal accuracy.
numbers: Budget K=512 traces; DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B; AIME24/25, BRUMO25, HMMT25. DeepConf-low saves 43-79% of tokens (mean 62.88% on DeepSeek-8B), DeepConf-high 18-59% (mean 47.67%). Headline: AIME25 offline 99.9% (GPT-OSS-120B) vs 97.0% majority; up to 84.7% fewer tokens (HMMT25 row: 3.23 -> 0.49 x 10^8 tokens, accuracy 97.1 -> 97.9).
limits: Aggressive filtering (top 10%) loses accuracy in some settings: Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9 points; GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 also drops. Authors admit models are sometimes highly confident on wrong traces. Needs token log-probs and a warmup set. Threshold ablation: savings up to 69.6% at the aggressive end, low variant loses 0.26 points, high variant keeps full accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-computed stop signal for single traces (G5). The conservative setting is the safe one. Overconfident wrong traces are the known failure.

source: Ong et al. (2024) RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data
finding: Learned routers send easy queries to a cheap model and hard ones to a strong model, cutting cost by over 2x at 90 to 95% of the strong model's quality, but only when the router's training data matches the test distribution.
numbers: MT Bench: score 8.8 at 50% of calls to GPT-4 = 95% of GPT-4 (9.3); cost cut up to 75% with augmented data; up to 3.66x cheaper at 95% GPT-4 quality. MMLU: 75 at CPT(50%) = 92% of GPT-4. GSM8K: 75 at CPT(50%) = 87%. Trained only on Chatbot Arena data, routers on MMLU and GSM8K performed at the level of random routing; adding in-domain labels gave about 20% fewer GPT-4 calls than random.
limits: Out-of-distribution routers equal random. Router quality tracks benchmark similarity to training data. Routes between two fixed models, not a budget on one model.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as adaptive stopping: a difficulty predictor must be fitted on the target problem class (our S0 gate). A gate trained elsewhere can be no better than random.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: The best test-time method depends on question difficulty. Allocating budget by model-estimated difficulty bin matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S*. Compute-optimal revisions and PRM search match best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute (e.g. 64 vs 256 generations). Difficulty = 5 bins by the base model's own pass rate (more predictive than MATH's hand labels), with two-fold cross-validation on the bins.
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate, which itself costs sampling. Authors did not combine PRM tree search with revisions. Small gains on the hardest problems with every scheme.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G12. Estimate difficulty from the model's own early samples, then choose the strategy per bin.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Test-time compute can replace pretraining compute only on easy and medium questions. On the hardest questions it gives little and more pretraining is better. Search can hurt on easy questions.
numbers: FLOPs-matched comparison against a 14x larger model: test-time compute wins on easy and intermediate questions, and on hard ones depending on inference load. Beam search vs best-of-N: on easy bins (levels 1-2) beam search gets worse as the budget rises (over-optimising the verifier); on levels 3-4 it beats best-of-N; on level 5 no method makes progress.
limits: One model family (PaLM 2), one benchmark (MATH). Verifier exploitation is the proposed cause on easy items.
agent_relevance: Confirms G12's foothold rule: below some base success rate extra thinking is wasted. Also warns that heavier search on easy items lowers accuracy.

source: Brown, Juravsky et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: With a perfect checker, more samples keep helping (coverage grows like a power law). Without a checker, voting and reward models plateau, so the gap between what is reachable and what is picked grows.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples (beats the 43% single-sample SOTA). CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% -> 7.1% with 10,000 samples. MATH Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% (100 samples) -> 98.44% (10,000), but majority voting or reward model only 40.50% -> 41.41%.
limits: Gains rely on an automatic verifier (tests, proof checker). Voting plateaus near 100 samples. Selection, not generation, is the bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Agreement-based stopping cannot exceed what voting can find. Where a code check exists (G3), keep sampling until a real check passes; where none exists, stop early.

source: Zeng, Cheng, Yin, Zhou, Qiu (2025) Revisiting the Test-Time Scaling of o1-like Models
finding: For o1-like models (QwQ, R1-distill, LIMO) correct solutions are shorter than wrong ones for the same question, and longer chains hold more self-revisions that rarely fix errors. Parallel sampling gives better coverage than sequential revision.
numbers: Same-question mean length: correct < incorrect on MATH-500, AIME, Omni-MATH, GPQA. Share of revisions that keep the original wrong answer: R1-32B 72%, R1-14B 70%, R1-1.5B 58%, QwQ 32%, LIMO 54%. Successful-revision rate below 10% for QwQ, R1 and LIMO; for R1-32B/14B and LIMO accuracy gains plateau after about 10 revision steps. Shortest Majority Vote beats plain majority vote, mainly on AIME.
limits: Length-error link is partly confounded by hard questions drawing long chains. The per-model table values were garbled in the PDF text, so exact Shortest Majority Vote gains are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Conflicts with s1: forcing more 'Wait' is not safe on models that cannot revise well. Length can serve as a mild tie-breaker among agreeing answers, applied in code.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: cut thinking off at a cap, or append 'Wait' when the model tries to stop. Gives perfect length control and a modest accuracy lift for a 32B model fine-tuned on 1,000 traces.
numbers: s1-32B without vs with budget forcing (cap about 30k thinking tokens): AIME24 50.0 -> 56.7, MATH500 92.6 -> 93.0, GPQA Diamond 56.6 -> 59.6. Control: budget forcing 100%, token-conditional 40%, step-conditional 60%, class-conditional 50%, rejection sampling 100%. 'Wait' x2 on AIME24 53.3 vs 'Hmm' or 'Alternatively' 50.0. 'Wait' 1x/2x/4x on AIME24: 53.3/53.3/56.7.
limits: Gains flatten at 6x forced waits; too many causes repetitive loops. Benefit shown on a model fine-tuned for it. AIME24 has 30 questions, so one item is 3.3 points.
agent_relevance: Forced doubt helps only at the stopping edge and saturates. Consistent with G1: no doubt on a schedule; use it only to rescue a premature stop.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Sequential scaling beat parallel voting for the base model in their setup; yet resampling until the output fits a short length gave an inverse scaling trend, which is selection bias.
numbers: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct majority vote over 2 to 64 samples stays below s1-32B with budget forcing on AIME24. Rejection sampling to a length cap needed on average 655, 97, 8, 3, 2 and 1 tries per sample at caps of 3500, 4000, 5000, 8000 and 16000 thinking tokens; accuracy fell as the allowed length grew, because short outputs are those where the model was on the right track.
limits: Different base models in the two arms (fine-tuned vs not). Zeng et al. (2025) find the opposite ordering for o1-like models, so the result is not general.
agent_relevance: Short-and-right versus long-and-wrong is a selection effect, not proof that capping thinking helps. Do not cap blindly.

source: Chen, Xu, Liang et al. (2024) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge token counts on easy questions; later solution rounds rarely add accuracy. Training on shortened self-generated answers cuts tokens with little accuracy loss.
numbers: For 2+3: 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; one case produced 13 solutions. First solution round correct in over 92% of cases and uses under 60% of tokens (QwQ on ASDIV: first round 287 tokens = 38.7% of the response). SimPO with first-correct-solution plus reflection cut MATH500 tokens by 48.6% for QwQ-32B-Preview at maintained accuracy; ASDIV 96.9 -> 96.8 accuracy at 741.8 -> 381.6 tokens.
limits: Training-based fix, not a scaffold. Evaluated on QwQ-32B-Preview and an R1-style model. Harder sets (AIME24) keep more rounds.
agent_relevance: Supports G11: the first correct round is usually enough on easy items. A code check after round one can end early (S4 to S7).

source: Su, Healey, Nakov, Cardie (2025) Between Underthinking and Overthinking
finding: Length does not match difficulty: models think too long on easy items and too short on hard ones. Incorrect answers are much longer than correct ones. Training to prefer the shorter response (no correctness label) cuts length with small accuracy loss.
numbers: On MATH, incorrect responses average above 6,000 tokens vs under 3,000 for correct ones, for both models tested; strong negative Pearson and Spearman correlation between length and correctness. SimPO preferring shorter responses cut average length by about 30 to 60% with accuracy staying in an acceptable range; most of the cut came from shortening incorrect responses.
limits: Small models (R1-Distill, R1-Preview). No causal test. For zero-accuracy questions the lengths spread over a wide range, so length is a weak difficulty signal there.
agent_relevance: The model's own length is a poor difficulty meter, so budget should come from outside (code-computed agreement, early-sample pass rate), not from how long the model wants to think.

source: Gema, Hagele, Chen et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: Authors built tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy in frontier models. Five failure modes. Effects differ by model family.
numbers: Counting with five distractors, natural overthinking: DeepSeek R1 accuracy 70% -> 30%; Claude Opus 4 from near 100% to about 85-90%; o3 stable. Python-code distractors: Opus 4 from near-perfect to about 80%. Grades regression zero-shot: extended reasoning shifts to spurious features, and few-shot examples largely remove it. Zebra puzzles: all nine models degrade with more thinking. Survival-instinct item: a reported rate drops from 60% to 47% for Sonnet 4 with extended reasoning (metric label not confirmed).
limits: Tasks were built to expose the failure, so rates are not typical. Controlled budget prompts and natural length give different effect sizes (R1 drop mainly in natural). Authors say compute scaling still helps elsewhere.
agent_relevance: Second boundary for G11: on distractor-heavy or constraint-tracking tasks extra thinking can hurt. Few-shot examples fix some of it. Gate by task type.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012/2014) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Formal theory of when to stop computing: stop when the expected gain from one more computation is below its cost. The one-step greedy (myopic) rule stops too early; the optimal rule computes at least wherever the myopic rule does.
numbers: Theorem 7: if the myopic policy computes in a state, so does the optimal policy. Theorem 5: expected number of computations under the optimal policy is at most the value of perfect information divided by the cost per computation. One-armed Bernoulli example: at most (1-mu)/c - 3 <= 1/(4c) - 3 computations. VOI-based sampling beat UCB1 in 10,000-trial selection tests.
limits: Theory plus small simulations; assumes a known metalevel probability model. Bounds are loose.
agent_relevance: Gives the principled base for Adaptive-Consistency. Warns that 'stop if one more sample would not change the vote' is too eager. Keep a minimum sample floor (G6).

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Do the Right Thing: Studies in Limited Rationality
finding: Origin of value of computation: pick the computation with the largest expected net utility (decision-quality gain minus time cost). The single-step greedy form is the 'myopic' rule analysed by Hay et al.
numbers: Not opened. Cited through Hay et al. (2014), which names it the metalevel greedy approximation with single-step assumption.
limits: Book not read; claim from Hay et al. only.
agent_relevance: Theory name for G12's budget logic; cite as theory, not as an LLM result.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2020) Resource-rational analysis, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 43:e1
finding: Frame cognition as the best use of limited computation. The opened page was the Rahnev commentary on the target article, not the article itself. It states the main critique: the method can fit almost any data and drifts from a modelling tool into a claim that people are resource-rational.
numbers: No effect sizes on the opened page. Four named weaknesses: flexible fit, mischaracterised constraints, simple lab tasks, intractable rational benchmark.
quote: The computations required to establish the truly rational strategy are intractable and will always remain so.
limits: Target article's own numbers not read. Critique is from one commentator; the authors' reply was not read.
agent_relevance: Treat 'resource-rational' as a design lens, not proof that an adaptive stopping rule is optimal. Test each rule against fixed budgets.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control, PLOS Computational Biology
finding: Learned Value of Control model: people learn how much control to spend from reward, by learning the value of computation. It explained five published attention and Stroop/Flanker findings better than two simple learning models.
numbers: Model-fit BIC (lower is better): Lin et al. visual search, LVOC 1817.8 vs Rescorla-Wagner 9763.2 vs Win-Stay-Lose-Shift 3449.9. Krebs Stroop, LVOC 45.3 vs 1333.9 vs 2454.8; rewarded vs unrewarded 541 vs 691 ms, errors 4.9% vs 11.8%. Flanker (Braem): model predicted a 7 ms reward effect, observed 27 ms.
quote: According to the LVOC model, control allocation is a process of continuing gradual adjustment.
limits: Proof of concept. Only two rival models, no temporal-difference rival. Misses fast unlearning, ignores switch costs, predicted effect about 4x too small in Flanker. Fits are to published data. Page read in part (first 100,000 of 144,887 characters).
agent_relevance: Human control is adjusted gradually from the last level and learned from reward. A budget table that updates per problem class from outcomes mirrors this, but the match is untested.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long A Reasoning Model Thinks With Reinforcement Learning, COLM 2025
finding: RL-trained length control (LCPO) lets a 1.5B reasoner follow a token budget given in the prompt, and beats s1-style budget forcing at short budgets. The 'max' variant wastes fewer tokens on easy items.
numbers: L1 vs s1: 100-150% relative and 20-25% absolute gain at 512 and 1024 token budgets. Log-linear scaling slope 0.24 vs 0.37 for s1. L1-Exact about 1% below DeepScaleR-4K (unconstrained); L1-Max matches it with up to 2x fewer tokens. Out-of-domain (GPQA, LSAT, MMLU) length control still works; 1.5B L1 matches GPT-4o at equal length.
limits: Trained on math at 4K context. Length error is larger on MMLU-type tasks. The s1 gap is partly because s1 truncates mid-reasoning.
agent_relevance: Prompted budgets work if the model is trained for them. For an untrained model, enforce the budget in code (token cap plus forced answer), and prefer 'max' semantics over 'exact'.

source: CaRT (arXiv 2510.08517) as listed in SUBFIELDS.md
finding: Pointer kept from the project catalogue: a method for deciding when to stop reasoning. Not read here.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Unverified in this session.
agent_relevance: Open before adopting any learned stop gate in S0 or S6.

source: Cross-paper check: sequential vs parallel scaling (s1 against Zeng et al.)
finding: Two papers read this session disagree on direction. s1 says sequential 'Wait' extension beats voting for its fine-tuned model. Zeng et al. say parallel sampling beats sequential revision for QwQ, R1-distill and LIMO.
numbers: s1: majority voting on Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (2 to 64 samples) stays below s1-32B with budget forcing on AIME24. Zeng: 40 sequential revision steps vs 10 parallel samples, parallel gives higher coverage on AIME for QwQ and R1.
limits: Different models, base ability and revision prompts. Neither tested the other's setting.
agent_relevance: The result depends on whether the model can truly revise. Our schema (G11) bets on parallel and short; this is supported but not settled.

source: Cross-paper check: which stop signals survive
finding: Across ESC, Adaptive-Consistency, CISC and DeepConf the stop or weight signal that works is agreement or token-probability confidence computed in code. Verbal self-confidence is weak, and calibration scores mislead.
numbers: Reported savings: Adaptive-Consistency 1.9-4.4x fewer samples (accuracy change within 0.2 on average), ESC 34-84% fewer samples, CISC 41-46% fewer, DeepConf 18-79% fewer tokens. Verbal binary confidence: within-question discrimination 52.2%, CISC saving 10%.
limits: Baselines differ (40 samples, 512 traces, 10 samples), so savings are not comparable across rows. All numbers are from the authors' own papers. No independent replication was found in this session.
agent_relevance: Mark the savings [S] not [E] in the schema until a replication on our tasks.
